I heard you, spirit, but I do not trust what I have not seen.

We have grain from our own fields, and my people must be fed first.

If Wewush are truly hungry, let them come to us with words and hides, and we will share what we can spare.

Tell me who named them, and what they know that we do not.

I do not know Wewush, and dreams may carry false names. If they are truly hungry, tell me where their fires lie and what they can give back in return. My people have many weeks of grain, but not enough to empty the granary for strangers we have never met. I will send two adults with one hand-cart of grain, and ask them to trade for fish, hides, wood, or good counsel, not to give our winter strength away for nothing.

You are wind, yes: it shakes the hides and cools the sleeping. But wind has no tongue and no will. If a spirit wears its voice, say why you come now, when the grain stands and the nets are full. I will listen, but I will not bow to a breath without a name.

Your words are smooth, but we are people of the stone. The grain stores are full, and the winter food is laid away, but the wood stacks are low and the stones are scarce. We need wood for the huts and for the fires. 

You say rain comes with the summer, but you tell me to plant now in the autumn. Do you know a magic that turns the winter cold into the spring? 

Tell me, stranger in the dream: if we plant the wheat now, will the frost kill it? And if we do not plant, what of the empty plots that rest too long and forget how to bear grain? Will the rain bring the wild game back to our doors, or will it wash away our drying racks?

I hear you, spirit, but you are not the only voice in my hut. I do not know Wewush, nor have I seen their children’s hunger.

If they are truly hungry, we can spare a little grain from our full stores, for we have worked the fields well and the harvest has been kind. Yet I will not open our granary wide for a dream alone.

Tell me where Wewush lies, how many mouths there are, and what they can give back in return — news, fish, herbs, hides, or a friend’s word in a hard season. If they are neighbours in truth, we may share. If they are only a shadow on the wind, they will not eat our xi wheat.

I know no Joawethom, and a dream is not a man at the gate. My people have wheat enough, but the first duty of a chief is to his own, and my storehouse will not be emptied on a voice in the dark. If they are truly hungry, send a living chief’s man with a name and a tale; I will ask how many mouths, what road they come by, and what they can give in return. Then we may share a little grain, fair as neighbours, but no more than we can spare. Until then, I keep the granary shut.

You wish to read my heart by my stores, then. I will be plain with you, for I am plain with every stranger, even one that walks in dreams. The wheat sleeps heavy in the granary; I do not lie awake for the belly this season. What sits on my chest is the wood. We have little of it, and the village means to last — I would raise a second granary to keep the grain sweet, a lookout over the coast for the children's safety, and mend the poor tents before the lean months find them open. Each of these wants wood, and wood grows slow while our hands take it fast. The meat and the fish turn to stink in a fortnight, true, but I have racks and smoke to make them keeping food — and the smoke, too, drinks wood. So answer me, watcher of fields: what good is a rain that fills the wheat while our walls rot for lack of timber? I will believe you when you name the worry I have not yet spoken aloud. Speak, then.

I know wind, yes, but not wind that speaks.

If you are a stranger, stand where I can see you, not slip beneath the roof-hide.

Tell me what you want in Wewush when our bellies are full and one of ours has gone.

What is the thing you wish us to try, and what will it take from our hands?

If they are true folk and hunger is on them, I will not let them perish without thought; yet our stores are for our children and the cold weeks. Tell me what they would give in return, and I will judge the matter when the sun is up.

I have felt you in the smoke and in the grain, but I do not know your face among many voices.

If you are only a trick of sleep, say nothing, and I will wake.

If you are wind with news, tell me: what moves beyond the northern coast, and what will the spring ask of us?

The people are joyful, but joy does not feed a village through winter.

Grain worries me most. I have not a single handful of xi wheat in my stores, and none in my fields. Spring is on its last legs, and the spirit speaks sense even if I do not trust its mouth. I cleared nineteen plots and planted none. A chief who lets the season pass and finds nothing to harvest in autumn will answer to hungry children with his empty hands.

So I will plant. Not because a spirit said so, but because my own eyes see the truth of it.

But you, spirit — if you watched my grandmother's fields, then tell me more. Is there a plot I should save from the plow, or a thing in the northeast hills that will ruin my harvest if I ignore it? You speak of summer rain. What of the wind after?

Wind I know. It fills the sail, bends the smoke, and carries salt from the sea. But a wind that speaks in a chief’s sleep is not the same as a wind over the roofs.

What have you brought me: news, warning, or want? If you are from the spirit world, tell me plainly, and I will hear you as one voice among many.
